sentences.text: Gigantoraptor held the title of the largest known oviraptorosaur, with estimates placing its length between 8 and 8.6 meters and its body mass between 1.4 and 2 metric tons.
The preserved lower jaws of this animal measured 46 centimeters in length and were completely toothless.
Its forelimbs were notably long, featuring an elongated humerus that measured 73.5 centimeters and a slender hand.
Researchers proposed in 2007 that Gigantoraptor was likely partially naked, as its body mass was 300 times greater than that of smaller feathered dinosaurs.
Despite the potential loss of body feathers, scientists suggested the animal likely retained arm feathers for display and brooding eggs.
This species is linked to the discovery of giant oviraptorosaurian eggs up to 50 centimeters long, assigned to the oospecies Macroelongatoolithus carlylensis.
The existence of giant oviraptorosaurs like Gigantoraptor explains previous findings of very large eggs, up to 53 centimeters long, assigned to the oospecies Macroelongatoolithus carlylensis.
The first remains of Gigantoraptor were discovered in 2005 in the Iren Dabasu Formation of Inner Mongolia.
The type species Gigantoraptor erlianensis was formally named and described in 2007 by Xu, Tan Qingwei, Wang Jianmin, Zhao Xijin, and Tan Lin.
The shape of Gigantoraptor's beak suggests a generalist diet with potential occasional carnivory.
A 2007 histological analysis of the holotype fibula revealed seven preserved growth rings, indicating the animal's age at death.
The growth rings indicated the holotype died at approximately 11 years old and gained an average of 128 to 140 kilograms per year.
Researchers inferred that Gigantoraptor reached young adulthood at the age of 7 based on the spacing of its growth rings.
A 2017 study found that Gigantoraptor possessed the deepest beak among all caenagnathids.
The articular region of Gigantoraptor's jaws shows convergence with those of the modern tuatara.
The propalinal jaw movement and sharp dentary shelves suggest Gigantoraptor had a shearing bite capable of cutting plants and possibly meat.

Gigantoraptor had hind legs with proportions allowing rapid movement, was likely more agile than the known Tyrannosaurus, and had large claws, a combination not generally found in herbivores of that size.
The preserved jaw of Gigantoraptor indicates the theropod had a shearing bite, possibly for cutting plants or potentially meat.
The specimen has advanced ossification and growth rings in the perone indicating it was probably 11 years old when it died.
Although originally thought to be a basal oviraptorid, subsequent analyses have shown Gigantoraptor to be a caenagnathid.
In 2007, Xu and colleagues initially assigned Gigantoraptor to the Oviraptoridae in a basal position.
The genus Gigantoraptor was named by Xu and colleagues in 2007.
Gigantoraptor lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period.
Gigantoraptor fossils are found in the Iren Dabasu Formation of Inner Mongolia, dated to 95.8 ± 6.2 million years ago.
Gigantoraptor lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 83 to 70 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now Asia.
Despite its large size, Gigantoraptor was likely more bird-like than its smaller oviraptorosaurian relatives.
Later analyses found features like an elongated digit IV and curved claws that contradicted the hypothesis that Gigantoraptor was adapted for a cursorial lifestyle.
